questions.question: Which of the following administrative units was introduced during the reign of Shahjahan?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chakla**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• During the reign of Shahjahan, the administrative unit called **Chakla** was introduced.
 
• Chakla was a subdivision of a province (Subah) in the Mughal administrative system.
 
• Each Chakla was further divided into smaller units called **Paraganas**.
 
• The Chakla system aimed to streamline revenue collection and local governance.
 
• This administrative reform helped in better management and control of the vast Mughal Empire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Subah**

 
 
• Subah was the largest administrative division in the Mughal Empire, similar to a province.
 
• Each Subah was governed by a Subahdar who was responsible for law and order, as well as revenue collection.
 
 
 
• **Paragana**
 
 
• Paragana was a smaller administrative unit within a Chakla.
 
• It comprised several villages and was managed by local officials for tax collection and judicial matters.
 
 
 
• **Mahals**
 
 
• Mahals referred to revenue circles or estates within a Paragana.
 
• They were the basic units for land revenue assessment and collection.
 
 
 
• **Zamindars**
 
 
• Zamindars were landowners who collected taxes from the peasants and paid a portion to the Mughal administration.
 
• They played a crucial role in the revenue system of the Mughal Empire.

questions.question:
The Primary Deficit is zero in which of the following situations?

A. Fiscal Deficit is zero.

B. Interest payment is equal to Fiscal Deficit.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only B**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Primary Deficit is the fiscal deficit of a country excluding the interest payments on previous borrowings.
 
• The Primary Deficit is calculated as: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit - Interest Payments.
 
• If the interest payment is equal to the fiscal deficit, then Primary Deficit would be zero, since the entire fiscal deficit is accounted for by interest payments.
 
• Therefore, the Primary Deficit is zero when interest payment is equal to the fiscal deficit (Option B).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fiscal Deficit**: The difference between the government's total expenditure and its total receipts (excluding borrowing).
 
• **Interest Payments**: Payments made by the government to service its debt, i.e., the interest on loans taken in the past.
 
• **Budget Deficit**: When total government spending exceeds the revenue that the government generates, excluding money from borrowings.
 
• **Revenue Deficit**: The difference between the government's revenue expenditure and revenue receipts.
 
• **Understanding Deficits**: Tracking various types of deficits helps in understanding the financial health of the government and its ability to manage and service its debt.

questions.question: Which of the following States is a part of Panjnad (land of five rivers)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Punjab**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Punjab is known as the land of five rivers: Beas, Ravi, Sutlej, Chenab, and Jhelum.
 
• The name "Punjab" is derived from the Persian words "panj" (five) and "ab" (water), referring to the five major rivers in the region.
 
• The five rivers contribute significantly to the agricultural fertility of the state, making Punjab one of the most prosperous agricultural regions in India.
 
• These rivers eventually merge to form the Panjnad, which is a point where all five rivers combine.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Beas River**

 
 
• The Beas River is one of the five rivers of Punjab and flows through the states of Himachal Pradesh and Punjab.
 
• It is known for its historical significance as it marked the eastern extent of Alexander the Great's invasion in 326 BCE.
 
 
 
• **Ravi River**
 
 
• The Ravi River flows through the Indian state of Punjab and the Pakistani province of Punjab.
 
• It is one of the major tributaries of the Indus River system.
 
 
 
• **Sutlej River**
 
 
• The Sutlej River is the longest of the five rivers of Punjab.
 
• It originates from Lake Rakshastal in Tibet and flows through Himachal Pradesh and Punjab before entering Pakistan.
 
 
 
• **Chenab River**
 
 
• The Chenab River flows through the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir and the Pakistani province of Punjab.
 
• It is a major river of the Indus River system, and it merges with the Jhelum and Sutlej rivers in Pakistan.
 
 
 
• **Jhelum River**
 
 
• The Jhelum River flows through the Indian-administered territory of Jammu and Kashmir and the Pakistani province of Punjab.
 
• It is notable for its scenic beauty and historical importance as it passes through the Kashmir Valley.

questions.question: The Vernacular Press Act was enacted in which year in British India to limit the freedom of the Indian-language press?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1878**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Vernacular Press Act was enacted in 1878 by the British colonial government in India.
 
• It was implemented by the then Viceroy of India, Lord Lytton, to curb the freedom of the Indian-language press.
 
• The Act was aimed at stifling the criticism of British policies by the Indian press, especially those written in vernacular languages.
 
• Under this Act, the government had the authority to confiscate the printing press, paper, and other materials of a publication if it was found guilty of publishing seditious material against the British government.
 
• The Act faced severe opposition and criticism from Indian intellectuals and leaders, leading to its eventual repeal in 1881 by Lord Ripon.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lord Lytton**

 
 
• He served as the Viceroy of India from 1876 to 1880.
 
• His tenure was marked by controversial policies, including the Vernacular Press Act and the handling of the Great Famine of 1876–78.
 
 
 
• **Lord Ripon**
 
 
• He served as the Viceroy of India from 1880 to 1884.
 
• He is known for his liberal policies and for repealing the Vernacular Press Act in 1881.
 
• He also introduced the Ilbert Bill, which sought to allow Indian judges to try British offenders.
 
 
 
• **Indian Nationalism**
 
 
• The period during which the Vernacular Press Act was enacted saw a rise in Indian nationalism and the demand for civil liberties.
 
• Indian leaders and intellectuals used the press as a means to mobilize public opinion against colonial rule.
 
 
 
• **Press Freedom**
 
 
• The Vernacular Press Act is an important historical example of the struggle for press freedom in colonial India.
 
• It highlights the role of the press in advocating for political and social reforms.

questions.question: Madhavi Mudgal is a famous _______ dancer
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Odissi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Madhavi Mudgal is renowned for her expertise in **Odissi dance**, one of the eight classical dance forms of India.
 
• She has received numerous awards, including the prestigious **Sangeet Natak Akademi Award** in 2000 for her contribution to Odissi dance.
 
• Madhavi Mudgal has been instrumental in popularizing Odissi dance on global platforms through her performances and teaching.
 
• She trained under the guidance of Guru **Kelucharan Mohapatra**, a legendary figure in Odissi dance.
 
• Her choreography and performances are known for their grace, technical precision, and adherence to the traditional Odissi style.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Odissi Dance**

 
 
• Odissi is one of the oldest surviving dance forms of India, originating from the state of Odisha.
 
• It is characterized by its fluid movements, intricate footwork, and expressive gestures (mudras).
 
• Odissi dance is traditionally performed as a form of worship and storytelling, often depicting tales from Hindu mythology.
 
• The dance form is known for its distinct postures, such as the Tribhangi, which involves three bends in the body.
 
• Odissi music is based on classical Indian ragas and talas, adding a melodic dimension to the dance performances.
 
 
 
• **Sangeet Natak Akademi Award**
 
 
• It is the highest Indian recognition given to practicing artists for their outstanding contribution to performing arts.
 
• The award was established by the Sangeet Natak Akademi, India's National Academy for Music, Dance, and Drama, in 1952.
 
• Recipients of this award are honored for their work in fields such as music, dance, theater, and other performing arts.
 
• The award includes a citation, a plaque, and a cash prize, reflecting the recipient's exceptional talent and dedication.
 
 
 
• **Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra**
 
 
• He was a legendary Odissi dancer, choreographer, and teacher who played a crucial role in reviving and popularizing Odissi dance.
 
• Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra trained many renowned dancers, including Madhavi Mudgal and Sonal Mansingh.
 
• His contributions to Odissi dance earned him numerous accolades, including the Padma Vibhushan, India's second-highest civilian award.
 
• He is remembered for his innovative choreography, dedication to preserving traditional techniques, and nurturing new talent.

questions.question: Hill Area Development Programmes were initiated during the ______________ FiveYear Plan covering 15 districts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Hill Area Development Programme (HADP) was initiated during the Fifth Five-Year Plan in India.
 
• The program aimed at the development of hilly regions and covered 15 districts initially.
 
• The primary objective was to ensure the socio-economic development of these regions which are generally less developed compared to plains.
 
• Special emphasis was placed on improving infrastructure, agriculture, forestry, and human resource development in these areas.
 
• The program recognized the unique geographical and environmental challenges faced by hill areas and aimed to address them through targeted interventions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Five-Year Plans in India**

 
 
• The Five-Year Plans were centralized and integrated national economic programs.
 
• They were developed and executed by the Planning Commission of India, which was established in 1950.
 
• The plans aimed to boost the economy through various sector-specific schemes and policies.
 
• Each plan focused on different sectors like agriculture, industry, services, and social development.
 
 
 
• **Fifth Five-Year Plan (1974-1979)**
 
 
• This plan focused on poverty alleviation and self-reliance as the main objectives.
 
• It emphasized employment generation and the development of infrastructure.
 
• It also focused on agricultural growth and improving the living standards of the rural population.
 
 
 
• **Hill Area Development**
 
 
• Hill areas often face issues like soil erosion, deforestation, and inadequate infrastructure.
 
• Development programs aim to address these issues through sustainable practices.
 
• Efforts include promoting terrace farming, reforestation, and developing road connectivity.
 
 
 
• **Sustainable Development**

• It involves using resources in a way that meets current needs without compromising future generations.
 
• Key practices include eco-friendly tourism, organic farming, and renewable energy projects.

questions.question: What is the percentage of the disabled population in India according to the 2011 census?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2.21%**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• According to the 2011 Census of India, approximately 2.21__**% of the population** was recorded as disabled.
 
• This percentage translates to around **26.8 million people** with disabilities.
 
• The disabled population includes individuals with various types of disabilities like seeing, hearing, speech, movement, mental retardation, mental illness, multiple disabilities, and other disabilities.
 
• The census data is crucial for understanding the **distribution and needs** of the disabled population for policy formulation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of Disabilities**

 
 
• **Seeing Disability:** Includes blindness and low vision.
 
• **Hearing Disability:** Includes deafness and hard of hearing.
 
• **Movement Disability:** Includes locomotor disabilities affecting limbs, spine, etc.
 
• **Mental Disability:** Includes mental retardation and mental illness.
 
 
 
• **Policies for Disabled**
 
 
• The **Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016** aims to uphold the dignity of every person in society and prevent discrimination.
 
• The Act increased the number of recognized disabilities from 7 to 21.
 
• It guarantees access to inclusive education, employment, and social security for persons with disabilities.
 
 
 
• **Global Perspective**
 
 
• The **World Health Organization (WHO)** estimates that over 1 billion people globally live with some form of disability.
 
• Approximately 15% of the world's population experiences moderate to severe disability.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives**
 
 
• Initiatives like the **Accessible India Campaign** aim to make public spaces accessible to persons with disabilities.
 
• The **Deendayal Disabled Rehabilitation Scheme (DDRS)** supports services for persons with disabilities.
 
• Various scholarships and vocational training programs are available for empowering the disabled population.

questions.question: Identify a structure that plays a role in motility.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Flagella**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Flagella** are long, whip-like structures that protrude from the cell body of certain prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, aiding in cell motility.
 
• They are primarily composed of a protein called **flagellin** in prokaryotes and **microtubules** arranged in a 9+2 arrangement in eukaryotes.
 
• Flagella move in a propeller-like motion to propel the cell through its environment, essential for the locomotion of many bacteria and sperm cells.
 
• In bacteria, flagella can be located at one end of the cell (polar), both ends (amphitrichous), or all over the cell surface (peritrichous).
 
• The rotation of the flagella is powered by a motor protein complex located at the base of the flagellum, driven by the flow of protons across the cell membrane.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pili**

 
 
• Pili are short, hair-like structures on the surface of prokaryotic cells that are involved in attachment to surfaces and in conjugation (DNA transfer between cells).
 
• Pili are made of a protein called pilin and are not involved in motility.
 
 
 
• **Villi**
 
 
• Villi are small, finger-like projections found in the small intestine of many vertebrates.
 
• They increase the surface area for absorption of nutrients.
 
 
 
• **Fimbriae**
 
 
• Fimbriae are similar to pili but are typically more numerous and shorter.
 
• They are used by bacteria to adhere to host cells and surfaces, aiding in colonization and infection.
 
 
 
• **Cilia**
 
 
• Cilia are short, hair-like structures found on the surface of eukaryotic cells.
 
• They can move in a coordinated manner to move fluid or mucus over the cell surface or to propel single-celled organisms.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct about the rule of Chandragupta II?

A) Chandragupta II adopted the title ‘Vikramaditya’.

B) Kalidasa and Amarasimha were part of his court.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**option 4**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Chandragupta II** was one of the most powerful emperors of the Gupta Empire in India.
 
• He adopted the title **'Vikramaditya'**, which signifies valor and is associated with a legendary king of ancient India.
 
• His reign is often considered a golden age of cultural and scholarly achievements in ancient India.
 
• Renowned scholars and poets such as **Kalidasa and Amarasimha** were part of his court.
 
• Chandragupta II's rule was marked by significant advancements in science, art, and literature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gupta Empire:**

 
 
• The Gupta Empire existed from approximately 320 to 550 CE and is known for its significant contributions to arts, science, and political organization.
 
• This period is often referred to as the Golden Age of India due to its advancements and prosperity.
 
 
 
• **Kalidasa:**
 
 
• He was a classical Sanskrit writer, widely regarded as the greatest poet and dramatist in the Sanskrit language.
 
• Notable works include 'Shakuntala,' 'Meghaduta,' and 'Raghuvamsha.'
 
 
 
• **Amarasimha:**
 
 
• He was an ancient Indian scholar and author of the 'Amarakosha,' a lexicon in Sanskrit.
 
• The 'Amarakosha' is an important source for understanding classical Sanskrit and Indian culture.
 
 
 
• **Vikramaditya:**
 
 
• The title 'Vikramaditya' is often used by Indian kings to signify their valor and heroism.
 
• Chandragupta II's adoption of this title reflected his status and achievements.
 
 
 
• **Golden Age of India:**
 
 
• This term refers to a period of great cultural, scientific, and economic prosperity in Indian history.
 
• The Gupta period is considered the epitome of this era.

questions.question: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was the leader of which major peasant movement in 1928?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bardoli Satyagraha**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928 was a major peasant movement in India led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
 
• The movement was a non-violent protest against the increased land revenue assessment by the British government.
 
• Patel successfully organized the peasants of Bardoli taluka in Gujarat to refuse payment of the increased taxes.
 
• Due to his successful leadership, Patel earned the title "Sardar" which means leader or chief.
 
• The success of the Bardoli Satyagraha played a key role in the Indian independence movement by highlighting the strength of non-violent resistance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel**

 
 
• Sardar Patel was an influential leader in the Indian independence movement and later became the first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister of India.
 
• He played a crucial role in the integration of over 500 princely states into the Indian Union after independence.
 
• Patel is often referred to as the "Iron Man of India" for his decisive leadership and efforts in unifying India.
 
• He was awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, posthumously in 1991.
 
 
 
• **Non-Violent Resistance**
 
 
• Non-violent resistance, also known as Satyagraha, was a fundamental strategy in the Indian independence movement led by Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• This approach involved peaceful protests, civil disobedience, and non-cooperation with the British authorities.
 
• The philosophy of non-violence was rooted in the idea of achieving political and social change without the use of force.
 
• Satyagraha movements, such as the Bardoli Satyagraha, demonstrated the power of collective non-violent action.
 
 
 
• **Land Revenue System in British India**
 
 
• The British colonial administration in India implemented various land revenue systems, such as the Zamindari, Ryotwari, and Mahalwari systems.
 
• These systems often led to high tax burdens on peasants, resulting in widespread discontent and resistance.
 
• The Bardoli Satyagraha was a direct response to the excessive tax demands under the British land revenue policies.
 
• Movements against land revenue assessments became a significant part of the broader struggle for independence.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Bardoli Satyagraha**
 
 
• The success of the Bardoli Satyagraha boosted the morale of the Indian independence movement and demonstrated the effectiveness of non-violent resistance.
 
• It also led to the rollback of the increased land revenue assessment by the British government.
 
• The movement strengthened Sardar Patel's position as a key leader in the Indian National Congress.
 
• The Bardoli Satyagraha became a model for future peasant movements and non-violent protests in India.

questions.question: Who has assumed charge as the Chairman of ISRO in January 2022?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **S Somanath** assumed charge as the Chairman of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) in January 2022.
 
• Prior to this role, he was the Director of the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC) in Thiruvananthapuram.
 
• S Somanath succeeded **K Sivan**, who served as ISRO Chairman from January 2018 to January 2022.
 
• S Somanath has a strong background in aerospace engineering, particularly in the area of launch vehicle design and development.
 
• He has been associated with ISRO since 1985 and has contributed significantly to various space missions, including the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) and the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)**

 
 
• ISRO is the space agency of the Government of India, headquartered in Bengaluru.
 
• Founded in 1969, its vision is to "harness space technology for national development while pursuing space science research and planetary exploration."
 
• ISRO has launched numerous missions, including the Chandrayaan and Mangalyaan missions, which have significantly contributed to space research and exploration.
 
• ISRO operates a series of satellite launch vehicles, including the PSLV and GSLV, to deploy satellites into various orbits.
 
 
 
• **Launch Vehicles**
 
 
• The PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle) is known for its reliability and versatility in deploying satellites into polar orbits.
 
• The GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle) is used for launching heavier payloads into geostationary orbits.
 
• ISRO is also developing the GSLV Mk III, which is intended for future crewed space missions under the Gaganyaan program.
 
 
 
• **Chandrayaan Missions**
 
 
• Chandrayaan-1, launched in 2008, was India's first lunar probe and helped confirm the presence of water/hydroxyl on the Moon.
 
• Chandrayaan-2, launched in 2019, aimed to explore the lunar south pole region with an orbiter, lander, and rover, although the lander crash-landed.
 
 
 
• **Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission)**
 
 
• Launched in 2013, it made India the first Asian country to reach Mars orbit and the first nation globally to do so on its first attempt.
 
• The mission's primary objective was to develop the technologies required for interplanetary missions.

questions.question: Which type of rocks is formed at relatively high temperatures and by crystallization of solids?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Igneous rocks**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Igneous rocks are formed by the solidification and crystallization of molten magma or lava.
 
• These rocks can form beneath the Earth's surface (intrusive) or on the surface as a result of volcanic activity (extrusive).
 
• They are primarily composed of silicate minerals, including quartz, feldspar, and mica.
 
• Igneous rocks are classified based on their texture and composition, with common types being granite (intrusive) and basalt (extrusive).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of Igneous Rocks:**

 
 
• **Intrusive Igneous Rocks:** These rocks form from magma that cools slowly beneath the Earth's surface, resulting in coarse-grained textures. Example: Granite.
 
• **Extrusive Igneous Rocks:** These rocks form from lava that cools quickly on the Earth's surface, resulting in fine-grained textures. Example: Basalt.
 
 
 
• **Formation Process:** The formation of igneous rocks involves the cooling and solidification of molten material, which can originate from deep within the Earth's mantle or crust.
 
• **Mineral Composition:** Common minerals found in igneous rocks include quartz, feldspar, mica, and olivine. The specific mineral composition determines the rock's properties and classification.
 
• **Uses of Igneous Rocks:** Due to their hardness and durability, igneous rocks are widely used in construction (e.g., granite for countertops and building stones) and in the production of aggregates for concrete.

questions.question: Which of the following states emerged as a champion state under the Van Dhan Vikas Yojana in 2021?
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Manipur emerged as a champion state under the Van Dhan Vikas Yojana in 2021 due to its effective implementation of the scheme.
 
• The state set up numerous Van Dhan Vikas Kendras (VDVKs) to empower tribal communities by promoting value addition to forest products.
 
• Manipur's success was driven by its focus on capacity building, skill development, and market linkages for tribal entrepreneurs.
 
• The state has a significant tribal population that benefited from the initiatives aimed at improving their socio-economic status.

questions.question: Who among the following coined the name oxygen for the element released by mercury oxide in 1779?
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Antoine Lavoisier is known as the "Father of Modern Chemistry".
 
• He coined the term "oxygen" in 1779 after conducting experiments with mercury oxide.
 
• Lavoisier demonstrated that oxygen is a key component in combustion and respiration.
 
• He also named hydrogen and helped reform chemical nomenclature.
 
• Lavoisier's work laid the foundation for the law of conservation of mass.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mercury Oxide Experiment:**

 
 
• Lavoisier heated mercury oxide and observed the release of a gas, which he identified as oxygen.
 
• This experiment debunked the phlogiston theory, which was the prevailing theory of combustion at the time.
 
 
 
• **Law of Conservation of Mass:**
 
 
• Lavoisier established that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
 
• This principle is fundamental to modern chemical equations and stoichiometry.
 
 
 
• **Chemical Nomenclature:**
 
 
• Lavoisier collaborated with other chemists to create a systematic method for naming chemical substances.
 
• This new nomenclature helped standardize chemical language and improve communication among scientists.
 
 
 
• **Lavoisier's Publications:**
 
 
• His notable works include "Traité Élémentaire de Chimie" (Elementary Treatise of Chemistry) published in 1789.
 
• This book is considered one of the first comprehensive chemistry textbooks and outlines the principles of the new chemistry.

questions.question: Which physicist was famous for the gold foil experiment?

• Ernest Rutherford, a New Zealand-born physicist, is widely recognized for the gold foil experiment conducted in 1909.
 
• This experiment led to the discovery of the atomic nucleus, fundamentally changing the understanding of atomic structure.

• The gold foil experiment disproved the plum pudding model proposed by J.J. Thomson, suggesting instead the nuclear model of the atom.

• **Atomic Model:**
 
 
• The experiment led to the proposal of the Rutherford model of the atom in 1911.
 
• This model suggested that electrons orbit a dense, positively charged nucleus, much like planets orbit the sun.
 
 
 
• **Nobel Prize:**
 
 
• Rutherford was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1908 for his investigations into the disintegration of elements and the chemistry of radioactive substances.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• Rutherford is often referred to as the "father of nuclear physics" due to his pioneering work in the field.

questions.question: Right to Protection of Life and Personal Liberty is given under which Article of the Indian Constitution?

• It ensures the protection of life and personal liberty for every individual in India.

• Article 21 has been interpreted broadly by the Supreme Court to include various derivative rights like the right to privacy, right to a clean environment, and right to health.

questions.question: Biotic potential is defined as:

options.text: the tendency of a population to decrease under extreme environmental conditions
the tendency of a population to remain constant under extreme environmental conditions
the ability of a population to survive and remain constant under ideal environmental conditions
the ability of a population to increase under ideal environmental conditions

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**the ability of a population to increase under ideal environmental conditions**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Biotic potential refers to the maximum reproductive capacity of a population under optimal environmental conditions.
 
• It is an indicator of how quickly a species can reproduce and expand its population size.
 
• Under ideal conditions, with no limiting factors such as food scarcity or disease, populations can grow exponentially.
 
• Biotic potential is influenced by factors like the number of offspring per reproductive event, the frequency of reproduction, and the age at first reproduction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Carrying Capacity**

 
 
• The maximum population size that an environment can sustain indefinitely given the available resources such as food and water.
 
• Carrying capacity is determined by both biotic and abiotic factors.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Resistance**
 
 
• The sum of environmental factors that restrict the biotic potential of an organism and impose a limit on the number of individuals in a population.
 
• Includes factors like predation, disease, and competition for resources.
 
 
 
• **Exponential Growth**
 
 
• A pattern of data that shows greater increases with passing time, creating a curve that represents exponential growth.
 
• Occurs when resources are abundant and environmental conditions are ideal.
 
 
 
• **Logistic Growth**
 
 
• Population growth that is initially exponential, but slows as the population approaches the carrying capacity of the environment.
 
• Results in an S-shaped curve when population size is plotted over time.

• The Gandhara School of Art flourished during the Kushan period, particularly under the rule of Kanishka the Great in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE.
 
• It is known for blending Greek, Roman, and Indian artistic influences, creating a unique style of Buddhist art.
 
• Sculptures from this school were primarily made from materials like stone, terracotta, and notably ivory.
 
• Ivory was a prized material used for its smooth texture and fine grain, which allowed for intricate detailing in the artwork.
 
• The use of ivory in Gandhara art reflects the high level of craftsmanship and the trade connections of the region with distant lands.

• **Gandhara Region**

 
 
• The Gandhara region covered parts of modern-day Pakistan and Afghanistan, particularly the Peshawar Valley and the Swat Valley.
 
• It served as a cultural crossroads for numerous civilizations including Greek, Persian, and Indian.
 
 
 
• **Features of Gandhara Art**
 
 
• Gandhara art is characterized by realistic representation of human figures, attention to anatomical details, and elaborate drapery styles.
 
• The art often depicts scenes from the life of Buddha, along with other Buddhist themes.
 
 
 
• **Influences**
 
 
• The Gandhara School of Art was heavily influenced by Hellenistic (Greek) art, evident in the naturalistic treatment of human figures and the use of contrapposto stance.
 
• Roman art also influenced the style, particularly in the depiction of clothing and physical features.
 
 
 
• **Important Sites**
 
 
• Key archaeological sites of Gandhara art include Taxila, Peshawar, Swat, and Bamiyan.
 
• These sites have yielded numerous artifacts including sculptures, stupas, and monasteries.
 
 
 
• **Significance**
 
 
• The Gandhara School of Art played a crucial role in the spread of Buddhist iconography and religious art across Asia.
 
• Its influence can be seen in the Buddhist art traditions of Central Asia, China, and Japan.

questions.question: The book ‘All Roads Lead to Ganga’ has been written by which famous author?

• **Literary Works**
 
 
• Some of his other famous books include *'The Room on the Roof'*, *'The Blue Umbrella'*, and *'A Flight of Pigeons'*.

• **Themes in Bond's Writings**
 
 
• Bond's works often explore themes of nature, love, and the simplicity of rural life.

• **Bond's Influence**
 
 
• Ruskin Bond has inspired generations of readers and writers with his storytelling and descriptive writing style.
 
• He remains a beloved figure in Indian literature, especially among young readers.

__
 
• **Indus and Ravi**: The Ravi River is one of the five rivers of Punjab in northwestern India and eastern Pakistan. It is a significant tributary of the Indus River.
 
• **Yamuna and Hindon**: The Hindon River is a tributary of the Yamuna River in India, contributing to the Yamuna's flow.
 
• **Kali and Gori**: The Kali River, also known as the Sharda River, has a notable tributary called the Gori River.

• **Indus River System**

 
 
• The Indus River is one of the longest rivers in the world, flowing through China, India, and Pakistan.
 
• Major tributaries include the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej rivers.
 
• The river plays a crucial role in the agricultural economy of Pakistan.
 
 
 
• **Yamuna River**
 
 
• The Yamuna is the second-largest tributary river of the Ganges by discharge and the longest tributary in India.
 
• It flows through several states, including Uttarakhand, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Delhi.
 
• Major tributaries include the Tons, Chambal, Sindh, Betwa, and Ken rivers.
 
 
 
• **Kali River (Sharda River)**
 
 
• The Kali River flows through the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand, forming a natural border between India and Nepal.
 
• It is known as the Sharda River in the lower course and is vital for hydroelectric power generation and irrigation.
 
 
 
• **Narmada River**
 
 
• The Narmada is one of the major rivers in central India, flowing westwards over a distance of about 1,312 km.
 
• It is also known as the "Life Line of Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat" for its significant contribution to the state's water resources.
 
• Major tributaries include the Tawa, Hiran, Barna, and Dudhi rivers.

questions.question: Birsa Munda International Hockey Stadium, which is also the largest seated hockey stadium in the world, is situated in which of the following states?

• The Birsa Munda International Hockey Stadium is located in Rourkela, Odisha, India.
 
• It is recognized as the largest seated hockey stadium in the world, with a capacity of over 20,000 spectators.
 
• The stadium was built to host the 2023 Men's FIH Hockey World Cup, alongside the Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar.
 
• Named after the tribal freedom fighter Birsa Munda, the stadium aims to promote hockey in the region and provide world-class facilities for players and fans.

• The 2023 Men's FIH Hockey World Cup was hosted in Odisha, India, from January 13 to January 29, 2023.
 
• The tournament was played at two venues: Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar and Birsa Munda International Hockey Stadium in Rourkela.
 
• The event featured 16 teams from around the world, competing for the prestigious title.
 
• India has a rich history in field hockey, having won multiple Olympic medals and World Cups.
 
 
 
• **Birsa Munda**
 
 
• Birsa Munda was a prominent tribal leader and freedom fighter in India.
 
• He played a significant role in the Indian independence movement against British colonial rule.
 
• His legacy is celebrated, particularly in the states of Jharkhand and Odisha, where he led the Munda Rebellion.
 
• The stadium is named in his honor to commemorate his contributions to the country and his fight for tribal rights.

• The state government has partnered with Hockey India to promote the sport at the grassroots level.
 
• Odisha's commitment to hockey includes sponsoring the Indian national hockey teams and hosting major international tournaments.
 
• The development of world-class facilities like the Birsa Munda International Hockey Stadium is part of this broader strategy.
 
 
 
• **Biju Patnaik University of Technology (BPUT)**
 
 
• BPUT is a public state university located in Rourkela, Odisha.
 
• Established in 2002, it offers undergraduate and postgraduate degrees in various engineering and technical disciplines.
 
• The Birsa Munda International Hockey Stadium is situated within the university campus, providing easy access for students and the local community.

questions.question: Which of the following festivals is celebrated to welcome the spring season in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Holi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Holi, also known as the "Festival of Colors," is celebrated to welcome the arrival of spring in India.
 
• This festival usually falls in the month of March, marking the end of winter and the beginning of the spring harvest season.
 
• Holi signifies the victory of good over evil, commemorating the legend of Prahlad and Holika.
 
• People celebrate by throwing colored powders, singing and dancing, and enjoying festive foods and sweets.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Historical Significance:**

 
 
• The festival has its roots in ancient Indian mythology, particularly the legend of King Hiranyakashipu, his son Prahlad, and Holika.
 
• It symbolizes the triumph of good (Prahlad) over evil (Hiranyakashipu and Holika).
 
 
 
• **Cultural Practices:**
 
 
• On the eve of Holi, people light bonfires, known as Holika Dahan, to symbolize the burning away of evil spirits.
 
• The next day, people celebrate with vibrant colors, water balloons, and joyous gatherings.
 
 
 
• **Regional Variations:**
 
 
• Holi is celebrated differently across various regions of India, with unique traditions and customs.
 
• In Mathura and Vrindavan, the festival is celebrated with great fervor, commemorating the divine love of Radha and Krishna.
 
 
 
• **Global Celebration:**
 
 
• Holi has gained international popularity, with celebrations taking place in many countries around the world.
 
• It serves as a cultural bridge, promoting Indian traditions and values globally.

questions.question: What is the name of the solution that is employed to identify the existence of starch in food?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iodine solution**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Iodine solution is used to test for the presence of starch in food items.
 
• When iodine solution is added to a sample containing starch, the solution changes its color to blue-black.
 
• This color change is due to the formation of a starch-iodine complex.
 
• The test is simple and widely used in both educational and laboratory settings.
 
• It is a qualitative test, indicating the presence or absence of starch rather than measuring the amount.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Starch**

 
 
• Starch is a carbohydrate consisting of a large number of glucose units joined by glycosidic bonds.
 
• It is produced by most green plants as an energy store.
 
• Common sources of starch include potatoes, rice, and wheat.
 
• In the human diet, starch is a major source of energy.
 
 
 
• **Iodine Solution**
 
 
• Iodine solution, also known as Lugol's iodine, consists of iodine and potassium iodide dissolved in water.
 
• It is commonly used in medical and biological applications.
 
• Besides testing for starch, it is used as a disinfectant and antiseptic.
 
 
 
• **Starch-Iodine Complex**
 
 
• The blue-black color observed in the test is due to the formation of a starch-iodine complex.
 
• This complex forms when iodine molecules fit inside the helical structure of the amylose component of starch.
 
• The exact nature of this complex is still a subject of research, but it is believed that the iodine gets trapped in the helical structure, leading to the color change.
 
 
 
• **Other Tests for Carbohydrates**
 
 
• Benedict's test is used to identify reducing sugars.
 
• Fehling's test also identifies reducing sugars.
 
• Barfoed's test differentiates between monosaccharides and disaccharides.
 
• Each test has a specific reagent and mechanism for detecting different types of carbohydrates.

questions.question: Which of the following is a reason for India trade deficit?

options.text: India’s exports and imports are equal
India’s imports are less than its exports
India’s exports are less than its imports

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**India's exports are less than its imports**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• India has a trade deficit when the value of its imports exceeds the value of its exports.
 
• The trade deficit indicates that India is spending more on foreign trade than it is earning.
 
• This situation can be due to higher demand for foreign goods and services compared to domestic production.
 
• Persistent trade deficits can lead to a depletion of foreign exchange reserves and impact the overall economic stability.
 
• Major contributors to India's imports include crude oil, gold, and electronics, which often surpass export revenues.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Balance of Trade (BoT):**

 
 
• It is the difference between a country's exports and imports of goods over a specific period.
 
• A positive BoT is known as a trade surplus, while a negative BoT is known as a trade deficit.
 
 
 
• **Current Account Deficit (CAD):**
 
 
• It occurs when a country’s total imports of goods, services, and transfers exceed its total export revenues.
 
• CAD is a broader measure than the trade deficit as it includes trade in goods and services as well as unilateral transfers.
 
 
 
• **Foreign Exchange Reserves:**
 
 
• These are assets held by a country's central bank in foreign currencies, used to back liabilities and influence monetary policy.
 
• They include foreign banknotes, deposits, bonds, treasury bills, and other government securities.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Trade Deficit:**
 
 
• Prolonged trade deficits can weaken a country’s currency value relative to other currencies.
 
• It can lead to increased borrowing from foreign sources, contributing to national debt.
 
 
 
• **Trade Policy Measures:**
 
 
• Governments may implement tariffs, quotas, and subsidies to control the trade deficit.
 
• Encouraging domestic production and export-oriented industries are common strategies to reduce trade deficits.

• The story centers around a young girl named **Binya** who lives in a small village in the hills of Garhwal.
 
• Binya exchanges her leopard-claw pendant for a beautiful blue umbrella, which becomes the envy of the village.
 
• The novel explores themes of **innocence, jealousy, and the simple joys of life** in a rural setting.
 
• **The Blue Umbrella** was adapted into a film in 2005, directed by Vishal Bhardwaj, which won the National Film Award for Best Children's Film.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ruskin Bond**

 
 
• He is an Indian author of British descent, born on May 19, 1934.
 
• Bond has written over 500 short stories, essays, and novels, including 64 books for children.
 
• He received the **Sahitya Akademi Award** in 1992 for his novel "Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra".
 
• In 1999, he was awarded the **Padma Shri**, and in 2014, he received the **Padma Bhushan** for his contributions to literature.
 
 
 
• **Other Notable Works by Ruskin Bond**
 
 
• "The Room on the Roof" – His first novel, which won the John Llewellyn Rhys Prize in 1957.
 
• "A Flight of Pigeons" – A historical novella set during the Indian Rebellion of 1857.
 
• "The Night Train at Deoli and Other Stories" – A collection of short stories that capture the essence of life in small Indian towns.
 
• "Rusty, the Boy from the Hills" – A series of stories about Rusty, a young boy growing up in Dehradun.
 
 
 
• **Adaptations of Ruskin Bond's Works**
 
 
• Several of Bond's stories have been adapted into films and television series, such as "The Blue Umbrella" and "7 Khoon Maaf".
 
• His story "Susanna's Seven Husbands" was adapted into the film "7 Khoon Maaf" directed by Vishal Bhardwaj.
 
• "Ek Tha Rusty", a television series based on his Rusty stories, aired on Doordarshan in the 1990s.
 
 
 
• **The Blue Umbrella – Film Adaptation**
 
 
• The film adaptation was released in 2005 and directed by Vishal Bhardwaj.
 
• It won the National Film Award for Best Children's Film in 2007.
 
• The film stars Shreya Sharma as Binya and Pankaj Kapur as Nand Kishore, a shopkeeper who becomes obsessed with the umbrella.
